media.name: Media type
media.why: The headline drop is mostly broadcast. Broadcast fell by 66,780 stories, 79% of the net loss of 84,298, and news fell by another 23,513. Social is the exception, up 154% (6,222 to 15,792), and print rose 12%. Without broadcast, volume is down 11.6% (151,448 to 133,930). Broadcast is about 70% of stories in both years, so small changes in broadcast schedules or sources move the headline. What the counts cannot tell you is whether fewer broadcast promotions aired or fewer broadcast sources were monitored. The media-type counts sum to slightly less than the daily total because of how stories are classified.

countries.name: Source country
countries.why: The US fell 38% and Canada 25%, while Australia rose 43% and moved from fourth to second. The UK is down 9% and Ireland is flat. Part of this may be real, for example Black Friday growing as a local event in Australia, and part may be the mix of sources monitored, which these counts cannot separate. Treat country moves as directional.

brands.name: Brand
brands.why: Amazon (-12%), Samsung (-11%), Costco (-10%) and Best Buy (-5%) held up about as well as the market or better. The big falls are in general retail and marketplaces: Walmart -58%, Target -50%, Macy's -63%, Kohl's -69%, Currys -70%, Lowe's -79% and eBay -82%, with Apple down 38%. As a result Amazon's lead over Walmart widened from 1.9 times to 4.0 times. The only clear risers are Australian, Kmart (+54%) and Myer (+116%), which fits the country shift. Entity counts can swing when sources or tagging change, so confirm large moves in the platform.

rows: Buy now pay later and financing
deals.name: Deal type
deals.why: Most mechanics moved with the market (non-broadcast down 11.6%): "% off" -13%, week-long events -13%, free shipping -12%, doorbusters and BOGO -2%, trade-in -4%. Early access fell furthest at -47%, from 185 to 111 stories per 1,000 non-broadcast stories. Rising against the tide: buy now pay later +31% (1,937 to 2,535), price match and record-low pricing +5%, and gifts +5%. One plausible reading is that starting early is now the norm, so "early" is less of a hook, while value assurances and financing are becoming the differentiators. We cannot test that from counts alone. The readership sample still shows "early" articles drawing the most readers, so the lower volume may be an opening.

themes.name: Category or theme
themes.why: Gaming (-7%), travel (-6%) and cars (-13%) held up better than the market. Electronics (-24%), food and drink (-24%) and fashion and beauty (-23%) fell most. Of the surrounding themes, economic pressure fell 31% and AI shopping 22%, while scam and fraud stories rose 2% against a falling market, lifting their share of non-broadcast stories from 4.8% to 5.5%. The fall in economic language suggests the tariff and inflation framing is a smaller part of the story this year, but that is an inference from counts.

retail.label: Retailers
retail.intro: For retailers such as Walmart, Target, Best Buy and Costco: you are fighting for share of voice against Amazon in a season that is mostly about price.

items.t: Claim a mechanic Amazon is not owning
items.why: Amazon has 45,371 stories against Walmart 11,323, Costco 3,124, Best Buy 3,287 and Target 931. Price match and record-low pricing (7,210), trade-in and member perks (4,496) and financing (2,535) are all far less crowded than "% off" (55,485).
items.do: Pick one differentiator and lead every announcement with it, instead of competing on generic discount language.

items.why: Costco is 35% positive and Target 44%, against 52% to 55% for Walmart, Amazon and Best Buy. Headlines that name a product and a price ("$510 vacuum for $140") are the ones being repeated. In the readership sample, explainers do best: "Walmart Will Have Three Major Shopping Events" (32,727 total readership) and a Costco best-times piece (30,587) were among the most read.
items.do: Replace "great deals" copy with named products, real prices and clear start and end dates.

items.why: Last year Black Friday week was 681,707 stories and the week after still ran at 378,232. Early-access language already appears in 14,904 stories.
items.do: Spread announcements across 23 to 30 Nov and hold a second wave for Cyber Monday and the tail.

brands.label: Consumer brands
brands.intro: For manufacturers whose products are the deal: Samsung, Apple, Sony, Nike and their peers. You appear in other people's promotions, so retailer partners shape your story.

items.t: Brief retail partners before the peak
items.why: Samsung (26,498 stories) and Apple (16,448) rank second and third, ahead of every retailer except Amazon, most likely because their products headline other retailers' deals. In a keyword scan of the readership sample, headlines naming Amazon carry 26% of total readership and Apple 7%.
items.do: Share approved price points, claims and product naming with key retail partners this week.

items.t: Read the sentiment behind the number
items.why: Samsung is 63% positive. Apple is 29% positive and 67% neutral, with 747 negative stories, the most of any brand tracked.
items.do: Pull the negative Apple-style stories for your own brand and find the pattern now, while there is time to respond.

items.t: Weight effort to the categories that are loud
items.why: Electronics lead (24,372), then fashion and beauty (18,124), home and kitchen (17,014) and gaming (16,917). Cars and EVs (14,210) and travel (11,899) show deals are not only gadgets.
items.do: Match launch support and ad spend to the categories where your mentions already cluster.

market.label: Marketplaces and sellers
market.intro: For marketplaces, DTC brands and third-party sellers such as Temu, Shein, Etsy and eBay: low volume, but the thinnest margin for a reputational hit.

items.t: Find out what drives the negatives now
items.why: Temu is 8.8% negative on 455 stories and Shein 4.9% on 506, the two highest shares among the brands tracked. Both are small against Amazon's 45,371.
items.do: Read the negative stories, categorise the themes and prepare holding statements before volume multiplies.

items.t: Put counterfeit and fake-deal risk on watch
items.why: Scam, fraud and fake-discount stories reach 7,418. A 5 Nov event warned sellers on Etsy and Amazon about brand risk ahead of Black Friday.
items.do: Set a watchlist of your brand plus scam, fake and counterfeit, and agree who responds and how.

items.t: Make delivery and value promises explicit
items.why: Free shipping and delivery appears in 6,872 stories and trade-in, cashback and member perks in 4,496.
items.do: State delivery cut-off dates and return terms up front, since these are the mechanics shoppers read about.

comms.label: Comms and PR
comms.intro: For in-house and agency teams trying to be heard: coverage is loud and most of it is promotional.

items.t: Lead with an angle, not another discount
items.why: Economic pressure (13,164 stories), scam warnings (7,418), AI shopping tools (6,996) and travel deals (11,899) run alongside the promotions. Many detected events are issuer press releases. In a keyword scan of the readership sample, articles framed around "early" deals drew 51% of total readership and guide-style pieces 15%, against 13% for percentage-off language. Articles tagged with AI have a median readership of 3,159, 2.7× the 1,158 overall.
items.do: Pitch data, consumer advice and trend angles instead of another sale announcement.

items.t: Match the channel to the goal
items.why: Broadcast is 301,925 of 435,855 stories (69%), News 101,702, Social 15,792.
items.do: Use broadcast for reach and promotion, and News for editorial credibility. Filter by media type when you report.

items.why: By source country the US leads (116,325), followed by Australia (90,333), the UK (86,529) and Canada (57,171).
items.do: Do not treat Black Friday as a US-only story. Adapt timing and offers for Australia, the UK and Canada.

items.t: Aim at the publishers people actually read
items.why: Lifehacker has average readership of 10,347 across 10 articles and Today 13,638 across 3, while Business Insider has 22 articles with a median readership of 67. Business and financial outlets are 17% of articles but 5% of total readership. Lifestyle and tech titles carry the attention.
items.do: Rank target publishers by average readership, not by how many pieces they publish. Lead with dated guides and early-access calendars.

risk.label: Risk and corporate affairs
risk.intro: For risk, legal and corporate affairs teams: the season brings workforce, safety and consumer-protection exposure as well as sales.

items.why: Signal detected stories on seasonal-worker injury risk (3 Nov) and, on 18 Nov, Starbucks and Amazon worker campaigns stepping up as the holidays approach.
items.do: Alert on your brand plus strike, walkout, injury and safety, and brief spokespeople before BF week.

items.t: Prepare for scam and fraud spikes
items.why: 7,418 stories already combine Black Friday or Cyber Monday with scam, fraud, phishing or fake-discount language. The one scam-warning piece in the readership sample (Fox News) drew 1,869 total readership, far below the 3,793 average across the sample.
items.do: Have customer-warning copy and a takedown route ready for fake sites and phishing using your name.

items.why: Consumer-protection guidance is already out (for example Brazil's Procon on 18 Nov) and fake-discount stories sit inside the 7,418.
items.do: Check "was and now" pricing and "lowest ever" claims against your price history before they go live.

RUN: Benchmark your share of voice against Amazon and two direct rivals
Lock your headline mechanic and proof points (named products, real prices)
Audit discount claims and "was and now" pricing before they go public
Set Signal alerts for brand with scam, counterfeit, strike and injury terms
23 to 29 Nov: Black Friday week, the peak
Check share of voice and sentiment daily against the 2025 peak shape above
Keep reactive statements approved for stock-outs, outages and fake-deal warnings
Stagger announcements across the week rather than one drop
30 Nov to 6 Dec: Cyber Monday and the tail
Pitch a post-Black-Friday angle: last year the following week still ran at 55% of peak
Capture results and sentiment drivers for the post-mortem
Feed the learnings into January sales planning
